chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, altogether from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), who said:

I said to him, 'A man does not know whether he has prayed one rak'ah or two.' He said, 'He should repeat (the prayer).' I said to him, 'A man did not know whether he had prayed two or three.' So he said, 'If the doubt enters him after he has entered the third rak'ah, he should proceed in the third, then pray the other (one), and there is nothing upon him, and he should offer Salam.' I said, 'So if he does not know whether he was in the second or the fourth?' He said, 'He should offer Salam, and stand, so he should pray two rak'ahs, then offer Salam, and there is nothing upon him.'

key_terms.شَكّ: Doubt or uncertainty regarding a specific detail of worship
key_terms.لَا شَيْ‏ءَ عَلَيْهِ: There is nothing upon him (no penalty or further obligation)
key_terms.يُسَلِّمُ: He offers the greeting of peace (concludes the prayer)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a person who doubts the number of rak'ahs they have prayed in Salah?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific jurisprudential rulings for doubt (shakk) in the number of rak'ahs during prayer, distinguishing between scenarios where one must repeat the prayer versus those where one proceeds with caution (i'tibar). It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on resolving uncertainty through precise procedural steps, such as offering Salam and standing again, to ensure the validity of the worship without excessive burden. The narration highlights the practical application of doubt rules in daily devotional life, ensuring congregational and individual prayers remain valid despite minor uncertainties.
